cases.abstract: Multimodal robot demonstrations contain alternative behaviors that must be represented without sacrificing action precision. We introduce Vector-Quantized Behavior Transformers (VQ-BeT), which learn discrete latent action representations rather than clustering actions directly. Residual quantization combines coarse action codes with finer corrections, allowing a transformer to predict actions or action chunks from observation histories, optionally conditioned on goal observations. A continuous offset refines decoded actions, and generation requires only one forward pass. Across simulated manipulation and locomotion tasks, VQ-BeT achieves competitive task performance and captures diverse behavior sequences; diffusion baselines retain advantages on some tasks, including unconditioned Image Kitchen and BlockPush. On a real mobile manipulator, VQ-BeT completes 19 of 30 two-task trials versus 11 of 30 for a modified transformer diffusion policy, despite similar standalone-task success. Its final success count is also at least three times the baseline's on each of four longer tasks. With all policies executed fully closed-loop, mean inference on an RTX A4000 takes 18.06 ms versus 573.49 ms for the diffusion baseline.
cases.results: On the real mobile manipulator, the separation between VQ-BeT and DiffusionPolicy-T is greater for sequential tasks than for isolated subtasks. VQ-BeT succeeds in 47 of 50 standalone trials versus 45 of 50 for the diffusion policy, but in 19 of 30 two-task trials versus 11 of 30. In all four longer tasks, its final success count is at least three times that of the diffusion baseline, with ten trials per task. The comparison uses a modified DiffusionPolicy-T and fully closed-loop execution for all policies because receding-horizon control fails on this robot. Under these conditions, mean inference time on an RTX A4000 is 18.06 ms for VQ-BeT versus 573.49 ms for DiffusionPolicy-T. VQ-BeT also closes the fridge and toaster in both possible orders. The results therefore combine higher sequence-completion rates with faster action inference and observed multimodality, rather than an advantage confined to standalone manipulation.

cases.abstract: Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) integrates a separately trained imitation policy into sparse-reward online robot learning. A critic selects between imitation and RL actions during both interaction and temporal-difference bootstrapping, letting imitation inform exploration and value targets without regularizing the actor toward demonstrations. Separate policies accommodate different encoder preferences in imitation and RL; a shallow vision-transformer critic and actor dropout improve pixel-based learning. IBRL matches regularized fine-tuning on simpler Meta-World tasks but outperforms fine-tuning and demonstration-oversampling baselines on harder Robomimic scenarios. With 50 demonstrations, it solves pixel-based Square within 500,000 interaction steps, while those baselines remain below 60% success. On real-robot cloth hanging, 30 demonstrations and 30,000 online steps produce 85% success in 20 evaluations, versus 65% for imitation, 35% for fine-tuning, and 15% for oversampling. Hardware training uses sparse success rewards and manual resets. Removing either imitation proposal reduces performance even with actor dropout, indicating that using imitation in both interaction and bootstrapping contributes beyond actor regularization.
cases.results: On cloth hanging, IBRL improves beyond the imitation reference while the two demonstration-based RL baselines fall below it. Given 30 demonstrations and 30,000 online interaction steps, IBRL achieves 85% success, compared with 65% for BC, 35% for regularized fine-tuning (RFT), and 15% for demonstration oversampling (RLPD). These scores come from 20 evaluations per method using the same initial conditions. The contrast distinguishes learning beyond the demonstrations from simply retaining their performance on this deformable-object task. Faster learning is also evident in Drawer: with 30 demonstrations, the checkpoint at 10,000 interaction steps achieves 100% success for IBRL, versus 15% for RFT and 0% for RLPD, again over 20 evaluations. All real-robot training uses only sparse binary success rewards, with manual resets between episodes.
